Calistoga, à l'extrême nord de la Napa Valley, est plus chaude encore, et donne certains des vins les plus mûrs et les plus amples. Les zones intérieures et plus chaudes de Sonoma peuvent donner des vins tout aussi puissants. Même étiquetés Cabernet Sauvignon, ces vins peuvent contenir de petites quantités d'autres cépages.

À l'autre bout de l'échelle, les vins étiquetés simplement California peuvent assembler des raisins de tout l'État, en grande partie issus des vignobles chauds et irrigués de la Central Valley. Ils sont faits pour être bus jeunes, et leur éventuel boisé vient en général de copeaux ou de douelles.

Au Chili, le Cabernet Sauvignon est le cépage le plus planté. Deux sous-régions clés se trouvent dans la vaste Central Valley : la Maipo Valley et la Colchagua Valley. Elles s'étendent des contreforts des Andes à l'est jusqu'à la cordillère côtière à l'ouest, avec des terres plus plates et plus fertiles en fond de vallée, ce qui offre aux producteurs un immense choix de sites. De plus en plus de domaines y font des Cabernets de très bons à excellents, seuls ou assemblés avec le Merlot et la spécialité chilienne, le Carmenère. Les vins des contreforts montrent souvent une menthe et un poivron vert caractéristiques, avec le fruit noir et le boisé.

En Afrique du Sud, Stellenbosch est une région montagneuse de grande qualité, où le climat va du modéré au chaud selon l'altitude et les brises marines. Les styles suivent : des Cabernets frais et herbacés jusqu'à des vins amples, au fruit cuit et riches en alcool. Cabernet et Merlot sont parfois assemblés avec le cépage local, le Pinotage, pour former ce qu'on appelle un Cape Blend.

En Australie, Margaret River, en Australie-Occidentale, est chaude mais tempérée par les brises côtières et d'abondantes pluies d'hiver. Son Cabernet, parfois assemblé avec du Merlot, montre un fruit noir mûr et un boisé subtil. Coonawarra, petite région d'Australie-Méridionale, est rafraîchie par la couverture nuageuse et les brises du sud. Son Cabernet a un caractère mentholé très reconnaissable, un cassis marqué, des notes de fumée et de cèdre venues du fût, et peut vieillir de nombreuses années. Enfin, dans la Hawke's Bay néo-zélandaise, au climat modéré, le Cabernet a besoin des sites les plus chauds pour mûrir et s'assemble en général avec le Merlot, plus répandu, pour donner un fruit rouge et noir frais avec une touche de poivron vert.

Une astuce pour retenir le Cabernet Sauvignon : imaginez un pied de cassis avec un brin de menthe, planté dans un lit de graviers. Le cassis, c'est son fruit, la menthe sa signature herbacée, et les graviers le sol chaud et drainant de la Rive Gauche qui l'aide à mûrir. Ajoutez une boîte en bois de cèdre pour le fût, et vous avez le portrait classique.

Avant le quiz, retenez trois choses. Premièrement, le Cabernet Sauvignon est un raisin noir à peau épaisse et à maturité tardive, pour climats modérés et chauds, qui donne des vins de couleur profonde, à l'acidité et aux tanins élevés, avec cassis, cerise noire et menthe ou poivron vert ; souvent élevé en fût, il peut vieillir des décennies. Deuxièmement, à Bordeaux, il domine les assemblages de la Rive Gauche, Haut-Médoc, Margaux, Pauillac, Graves et Pessac-Léognan, grâce aux graves chaudes et drainantes, avec plus de Merlot les années difficiles. Troisièmement, les grandes zones du Nouveau Monde incluent la Napa Valley avec Oakville, Rutherford et Calistoga, Sonoma, Maipo et Colchagua au Chili, Stellenbosch, Margaret River, Coonawarra et sa menthe, et Hawke's Bay.
en: In this lesson we meet one of the most famous red grapes on the planet: Cabernet Sauvignon. It is the backbone of the great wines of Bordeaux's Left Bank, and today outstanding examples come from almost every wine country. We will look at what the grape is like, why it so often spends time in oak and why it can age for decades. Then we tour its key regions: Bordeaux and the Languedoc in France, Napa Valley and Sonoma in California, Chile, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand.

First, the grape. Cabernet Sauvignon is a black variety from south-west France. Its grapes are small, with thick skins full of colour, flavour and tannin. It needs a long, warm growing season to ripen fully, so it grows in moderate and warm climates; in a moderate climate it can struggle to ripen except in the warmest sites. A single-varietal Cabernet Sauvignon is deeply coloured, dry, high in acidity, high in tannin and medium to full in body. Its signature is pronounced black fruit, blackcurrant and black cherry, usually with a herbal note of mint or a herbaceous note of green bell pepper. In very warm places the fruit can taste cooked.

In the winery, Cabernet Sauvignon is often blended, especially with Merlot. Merlot's softer, fleshier fruit fills in around Cabernet's firm structure and tames its very high tannin and acidity. This matters most in cooler years in moderate climates, when Cabernet may not ripen fully. Think of Cabernet Sauvignon as the frame of a house and Merlot as the furniture that makes it comfortable.

A freshly fermented Cabernet Sauvignon can taste harshly tannic. So it usually spends months or even years in oak barrels before bottling. The small amount of oxygen that passes through the barrel helps soften the tannins, and new oak adds secondary flavours of smoke, vanilla, cloves and cedar. Then comes the bottle. High tannin and acidity act as natural preservatives, so very good and outstanding wines can mature for many years. Over time the tannins soften and tertiary notes appear: dried fruit, earth and forest floor.

Now Bordeaux. The climate is moderate and maritime, and in its coolest sites Cabernet Sauvignon may not ripen reliably. The secret of the Left Bank, west and south of the Gironde estuary and the Garonne river, is gravel: stony soils that drain quickly after heavy rain and soak up heat during the day, keeping the vineyard warm into the evening. That extra warmth helps Cabernet ripen. Cabernet-dominated blends come from the Haut-Médoc, which includes famous villages like Margaux and Pauillac, and from Graves, which includes Pessac-Léognan. The best of these wines can age for a very long time.

Bordeaux's weather changes a lot from year to year. In some years Cabernet struggles to ripen even on the gravel, and that is where blending earns its keep: in a difficult year, the share of Merlot in the blend can go up. On Left Bank labels you may also see terms such as Château, Grand Cru Classé or Cru Bourgeois, which we cover in the lesson on label terms.

Still in France, the Languedoc-Roussillon is warm, and its weather is far more reliable than Bordeaux's, so Cabernet Sauvignon ripens every year. Here you will find both single-varietal Cabernet and blends with Merlot and other black grapes, usually labelled Pays d'Oc IGP.

Now California. The neighbouring regions of Napa Valley and Sonoma make many very good and outstanding Cabernets. Napa Valley has a warm, sunny climate and a long growing season, ideal for this grape. In the sub-regions of Oakville and Rutherford you find full-bodied wines with pronounced ripe black fruit and high, ripe tannins. Calistoga, in the far north of Napa Valley, is warmer still, and makes some of the ripest, fullest wines of all. The warmer inland parts of Sonoma can make similarly powerful wines. Even when labelled Cabernet Sauvignon, these wines may contain small amounts of other grapes.

At the other end of the scale, wines labelled simply California can be blended from grapes grown anywhere in the state, much of it from the hot, irrigated vineyards of the Central Valley. They are made to be drunk young, and any oak flavour usually comes from chips or staves.

In Chile, Cabernet Sauvignon is the most widely planted grape of all. Two key sub-regions sit within the broad Central Valley: the Maipo Valley and the Colchagua Valley. They stretch from the foothills of the Andes in the east to the coastal mountains in the west, with flatter, more fertile land on the valley floor, so producers have a huge choice of sites. More and more of them make very good to outstanding Cabernet Sauvignon, alone or blended with Merlot and Chile's speciality, Carmenère. Wines from the foothills often show distinctive mint and green pepper alongside black fruit and oak.

In South Africa, Stellenbosch is a high-quality, mountainous region where the climate goes from moderate to warm depending on altitude and sea breezes. So the styles range from fresh, herbal Cabernet to full-bodied wines with cooked fruit and high alcohol. Cabernet and Merlot are sometimes blended with the local grape Pinotage, to make what is known as a Cape Blend.

In Australia, Margaret River, in Western Australia, is warm but moderated by coastal breezes and plentiful winter rain. Its Cabernet, sometimes blended with Merlot, shows ripe black fruit and subtle oak. Coonawarra, a small region in South Australia, is cooled by cloud cover and southern breezes. Its Cabernet has a distinctive mint character, pronounced blackcurrant and smoke and cedar from oak, and can age for many years. Finally, in New Zealand's moderate Hawke's Bay, Cabernet needs the warmest sites to ripen, and is usually blended with the more widely grown Merlot, giving fresh red and black fruit with a hint of green pepper.

A memory tip for Cabernet Sauvignon: think of a blackcurrant bush with a sprig of mint, planted in a gravel bed. The blackcurrant is its fruit, the mint its herbal signature, and the gravel the warm, well-drained soil of the Left Bank that helps it ripen. Add a cedar box for the oak, and you have the classic picture.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Cabernet Sauvignon is a thick-skinned, late-ripening black grape for moderate and warm climates, giving deep-coloured wines with high acidity, high tannin, blackcurrant, black cherry and mint or green pepper; it is often oak-aged and can age for decades. Second, in Bordeaux it dominates the Left Bank blends of the Haut-Médoc, Margaux, Pauillac, Graves and Pessac-Léognan, thanks to warm, well-drained gravel, with Merlot added in difficult years. Third, key New World areas include Napa Valley with Oakville, Rutherford and Calistoga, Sonoma, Maipo and Colchagua in Chile, Stellenbosch, Margaret River, minty Coonawarra and Hawke's Bay.

it: In questa lezione incontriamo il grande compagno del Cabernet Sauvignon, nonché una stella a pieno titolo: il Merlot. Dalla sua patria, Bordeaux, si è diffuso in tutto il mondo. Può dare rossi leggeri e fruttati da godere subito, ma anche vini ricchi e concentrati che migliorano con il rovere e con gli anni di bottiglia. Vedremo com'è quest'uva, come la maturazione la cambia, perché è un compagno di taglio così prezioso, e poi visiteremo le sue zone chiave, da Saint-Émilion e Pomerol fino a California, Cile, Sudafrica, Australia e Nuova Zelanda.

Prima di tutto, l'uva. Il Merlot è una varietà a bacca nera che cresce nei climi temperati e caldi. Un Merlot in purezza è di solito secco, con acidità media e tannini medi: più morbido e rotondo del Cabernet Sauvignon. Il suo carattere dipende dalla maturazione. Un Merlot appena maturo dà vini di corpo leggero o medio, con frutto rosso fresco, fragola e prugna rossa, e un tocco erbaceo di peperone verde. Un Merlot più maturo dà vini di corpo medio o pieno, con frutto nero cotto, mora e prugna nera. Lo stile più maturo si ottiene facilmente in un clima caldo, ma si può raggiungere anche in un clima temperato vendemmiando più tardi.

In cantina il Merlot può dare vini eccellenti da solo, ma è anche un celebre vitigno da taglio. Unito a varietà più tanniche come il Cabernet Sauvignon, aggiunge frutto rosso e abbassa il tannino complessivo, così il vino è pronto da bere prima. Esistono stili con e senza legno. Un Merlot leggero e fruttato non ha bisogno di un lungo passaggio in botte. Uno stile più pieno può guadagnare morbidezza e complessità dal rovere. E i migliori vini a base di Merlot invecchiano bene, sviluppando note di frutta secca e tabacco.

Ora Bordeaux, la casa classica del Merlot, nel sud-ovest della Francia. Il clima è temperato, con piogge abbondanti per la vicinanza dell'Atlantico, e il Merlot è il vitigno più piantato della regione. La maggior parte dei vini sono tagli, soprattutto di Merlot e Cabernet Sauvignon. Le proporzioni dipendono dallo stile voluto, ma anche dai suoli e dal meteo di ogni annata: in un anno in cui il Cabernet fatica, nel taglio entra più Merlot.

Bordeaux è divisa dall'estuario della Gironda, dove si incontrano la Garonna e la Dordogna. A ovest e a sud di Gironda e Garonna c'è la Rive Gauche, con Médoc, Graves e Sauternes, dove di solito comanda il Cabernet Sauvignon. A nord e a est di Gironda e Dordogna c'è la Rive Droite, la riva destra, le cui zone chiave sono Saint-Émilion e Pomerol. Qui il re è il Merlot. I vini eccellenti di Saint-Émilion e Pomerol sono di corpo pieno, con frutto nero intenso e rovere, e invecchiano bene, sviluppando frutta secca e tabacco.

Una parola veloce sulle etichette di Bordeaux. Le denominazioni regionali, Bordeaux e Bordeaux Supérieur, possono usare uve da tutta la regione, e questi vini sono di solito tagli guidati dal Merlot. Il Bordeaux Supérieur ha regole un po' più severe del semplice Bordeaux su rese, affinamento e gradazione minima. Sulla Rive Droite, la denominazione Saint-Émilion comprende anche un livello più prestigioso, il Saint-Émilion Grand Cru.

Sempre in Francia, il Merlot è molto piantato nella calda Linguadoca-Rossiglione. Si trova Merlot in purezza a tutti i livelli di qualità, oltre a tagli con Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache e Syrah, di solito etichettati Pays d'Oc IGP.

Ora la California, fonte di Merlot in tutti gli stili e a tutti i livelli di qualità. I tagli sono comuni, ma conta anche il Merlot in purezza. Gli stili vanno da vini fruttati e di corpo medio, etichettati semplicemente California, a vini concentrati e di corpo pieno delle zone vicine di Napa Valley e Sonoma. I rossi californiani mostrano spesso aromi di legno evidenti, vaniglia, cocco e fumo. I migliori affinano spesso in botti nuove, mentre i grandi produttori possono usare trucioli o doghe.

In Cile, il Merlot matura facilmente nella calda e asciutta Central Valley, dove ogni anno si possono ottenere rese alte di uva perfettamente matura. Questo fa della Central Valley una fonte importante di Merlot morbido e di corpo medio per vini di marca in grandi volumi, da bere giovani. Ma l'altitudine può mitigare il caldo, e così si producono anche stili più freschi.

In Sudafrica, Stellenbosch si è costruita una solida fama per rossi complessi e longevi dalle classiche uve bordolesi, Merlot compreso. Questa zona montuosa va dal temperato al caldo, a seconda dell'altitudine dei vigneti e dell'influsso delle brezze marine. In Australia, il Merlot è tradizionalmente un compagno di taglio del Cabernet Sauvignon in vini di alta qualità, per esempio a Margaret River, nell'Australia Occidentale.

In Nuova Zelanda, la maggior parte del Merlot viene da Hawke's Bay, nell'Isola del Nord. Il clima è temperato, con piogge abbondanti. I vini vanno da leggeri e fruttati a pieni e longevi, e il Merlot si trova sia in purezza sia in taglio con il Cabernet Sauvignon. Anzi, lì è più diffuso del Cabernet, che ha bisogno dei siti più caldi.

Il Merlot è stato a volte considerato un'uva per vini di marca in grandi volumi, o solo un ammorbidente per il Cabernet Sauvignon. Oggi produttori di tutto il mondo dimostrano che da solo può dare vini importanti, complessi e longevi. Con tannino e acidità medi è un'uva meravigliosamente versatile: fresca e senza legno a qualunque prezzo, oppure potente e arricchita da rovere e bottiglia.

Un trucco per ricordare: se il Cabernet Sauvignon è una stretta di mano decisa, il Merlot è un abbraccio caldo. Tannini più morbidi, acidità media, prugne e frutti di bosco polposi. E per collocarlo sulla mappa, ricordate che la Rive Droite è la riva del Merlot: Saint-Émilion e Pomerol, dove l'abbraccio è più ricco.

Prima del quiz, ricordate tre cose. Primo, il Merlot è un'uva nera per climi temperati e caldi, che dà vini secchi con acidità e tannini medi; uve appena mature danno frutto rosso e peperone verde, uve più mature corpo più pieno e frutto nero cotto. Secondo, è il vitigno più piantato di Bordeaux e guida i vini della Rive Droite, Saint-Émilion e Pomerol, oltre alla maggior parte dei Bordeaux e Bordeaux Supérieur, mentre nei tagli ammorbidisce il Cabernet Sauvignon. Terzo, altrove va dai vini fruttati e in grandi volumi del Pays d'Oc, della California e della Central Valley cilena ai vini più pieni e affinati in rovere di Napa Valley e Sonoma, fino ai rossi e ai tagli di qualità di Stellenbosch, Margaret River e Hawke's Bay.
fr: Dans cette leçon, nous rencontrons le grand partenaire du Cabernet Sauvignon, et une star à part entière : le Merlot. Depuis sa terre natale bordelaise, il s'est répandu dans le monde entier. Il peut donner des rouges légers et fruités à boire tout de suite, mais aussi des vins riches et concentrés qui gagnent à l'élevage en fût et à des années de bouteille. Nous verrons à quoi ressemble ce cépage, comment la maturité le transforme, pourquoi c'est un si bon partenaire d'assemblage, puis nous visiterons ses régions clés, de Saint-Émilion et Pomerol jusqu'en Californie, au Chili, en Afrique du Sud, en Australie et en Nouvelle-Zélande.

D'abord, le cépage. Le Merlot est un raisin noir qui pousse en climat modéré et chaud. Un Merlot pur est en général sec, avec une acidité moyenne et des tanins moyens : plus souple et plus rond que le Cabernet Sauvignon. Son caractère dépend de la maturité. Un Merlot tout juste mûr donne des vins de corps léger à moyen, au fruit rouge frais, fraise et prune rouge, avec une touche herbacée de poivron vert. Un Merlot plus mûr donne des vins de corps moyen à ample, au fruit noir cuit, mûre et prune noire. Ce style plus mûr s'obtient facilement en climat chaud, mais on peut aussi l'atteindre en climat modéré en vendangeant plus tard.

Au chai, le Merlot peut donner seul d'excellents vins, mais c'est aussi un célèbre cépage d'assemblage. Associé à des cépages plus tanniques comme le Cabernet Sauvignon, il apporte du fruit rouge et réduit les tanins de l'ensemble, si bien que le vin est prêt à boire plus tôt. Il existe des styles boisés et non boisés. Un Merlot léger et fruité n'a guère besoin d'un long élevage en fût. Un style plus ample peut gagner en souplesse et en complexité grâce au chêne. Et les meilleurs vins dominés par le Merlot vieillissent bien, en développant des notes de fruits secs et de tabac.

Direction Bordeaux, la patrie classique du Merlot, dans le sud-ouest de la France. Le climat est modéré, avec beaucoup de pluie en raison de la proximité de l'Atlantique, et le Merlot est le cépage le plus planté de la région. La plupart des vins sont des assemblages, surtout de Merlot et de Cabernet Sauvignon. Les proportions dépendent du style voulu, mais aussi des sols et de la météo de chaque année : quand le Cabernet peine, on met plus de Merlot dans l'assemblage.

Bordeaux est partagé par l'estuaire de la Gironde, où se rejoignent la Garonne et la Dordogne. À l'ouest et au sud de la Gironde et de la Garonne se trouve la Rive Gauche, avec le Médoc, les Graves et Sauternes, où le Cabernet Sauvignon domine en général. Au nord et à l'est de la Gironde et de la Dordogne se trouve la Rive Droite, dont les zones clés sont Saint-Émilion et Pomerol. Là, le Merlot est roi. Les grands vins de Saint-Émilion et de Pomerol sont amples, avec un fruit noir marqué et un boisé présent, et vieillissent bien, en développant fruits secs et tabac.

Un mot rapide sur les étiquettes bordelaises. Les appellations régionales, Bordeaux et Bordeaux Supérieur, peuvent utiliser des raisins de toute la région, et ces vins sont en général des assemblages menés par le Merlot. Le Bordeaux Supérieur obéit à des règles un peu plus strictes que le simple Bordeaux sur les rendements, l'élevage et le degré minimum. Sur la Rive Droite, l'appellation Saint-Émilion comprend aussi un niveau plus prestigieux, le Saint-Émilion Grand Cru.

Toujours en France, le Merlot est très planté dans le Languedoc-Roussillon, au climat chaud. On y trouve du Merlot pur à tous les niveaux de qualité, ainsi que des assemblages avec le Cabernet Sauvignon, le Grenache et la Syrah, en général étiquetés Pays d'Oc IGP.

Passons à la Californie, source de Merlot dans tous les styles et à tous les niveaux de qualité. Les assemblages y sont courants, mais le Merlot pur compte aussi. Les styles vont de vins fruités de corps moyen, étiquetés simplement California, à des vins concentrés et amples des régions voisines de la Napa Valley et de Sonoma. Les rouges californiens montrent souvent un boisé marqué, vanille, noix de coco et fumée. Les meilleurs sont souvent élevés en fûts neufs, tandis que les gros producteurs peuvent utiliser copeaux ou douelles.

Au Chili, le Merlot mûrit facilement dans la Central Valley, chaude et sèche, où l'on peut obtenir chaque année de hauts rendements de raisins bien mûrs. La Central Valley est donc une source importante de Merlot souple et de corps moyen pour des vins de marque en grand volume, à boire jeunes. Mais l'altitude peut tempérer la chaleur, et l'on y fait aussi des styles plus frais.

En Afrique du Sud, Stellenbosch s'est forgé une solide réputation pour des rouges complexes et de garde issus des cépages bordelais classiques, dont le Merlot. Cette région montagneuse va du modéré au chaud, selon l'altitude des vignes et l'influence des brises marines. En Australie, le Merlot est traditionnellement un partenaire d'assemblage du Cabernet Sauvignon dans des vins de grande qualité, par exemple à Margaret River, en Australie-Occidentale.

En Nouvelle-Zélande, la plupart du Merlot vient de Hawke's Bay, sur l'île du Nord. Le climat est modéré, avec des pluies abondantes. Les vins vont du léger et fruité à l'ample et de longue garde, et le Merlot y est vinifié seul ou assemblé avec le Cabernet Sauvignon. Il y est d'ailleurs plus planté que le Cabernet, qui a besoin des sites les plus chauds.

On a parfois vu dans le Merlot un cépage pour vins de marque en grand volume, ou un simple adoucisseur du Cabernet Sauvignon. Aujourd'hui, des producteurs du monde entier montrent qu'il peut donner seul des vins impressionnants, complexes et de longue garde. Avec ses tanins et son acidité moyens, c'est un cépage merveilleusement polyvalent : frais et non boisé à tous les prix, ou puissant et enrichi par le fût et la bouteille.

Une astuce pour retenir : si le Cabernet Sauvignon est une poignée de main ferme, le Merlot est une accolade chaleureuse. Des tanins plus souples, une acidité moyenne, des prunes et des baies charnues. Et pour le situer sur la carte, retenez que la Rive Droite est la rive du Merlot : Saint-Émilion et Pomerol, là où l'accolade est la plus généreuse.

Avant le quiz, retenez trois choses. Premièrement, le Merlot est un raisin noir pour climats modérés et chauds, qui donne des vins secs à l'acidité et aux tanins moyens ; des raisins tout juste mûrs donnent fruit rouge et poivron vert, des raisins plus mûrs un corps plus ample et un fruit noir cuit. Deuxièmement, c'est le cépage le plus planté de Bordeaux, il mène les vins de la Rive Droite, Saint-Émilion et Pomerol, ainsi que la plupart des Bordeaux et Bordeaux Supérieur, et il assouplit le Cabernet Sauvignon dans les assemblages. Troisièmement, ailleurs il va des vins fruités et en grand volume du Pays d'Oc, de Californie et de la Central Valley chilienne aux vins plus amples et boisés de la Napa Valley et de Sonoma, jusqu'aux rouges et assemblages de qualité de Stellenbosch, Margaret River et Hawke's Bay.
en: In this lesson we meet Cabernet Sauvignon's great partner, and a star in its own right: Merlot. From its homeland in Bordeaux it has spread all over the world. It can make light, fruity reds to enjoy straight away, and also rich, concentrated wines that improve with oak and with years in bottle. We will see what the grape is like, how ripeness changes it, why it is such a good blending partner, and then we visit its key regions, from Saint-Émilion and Pomerol to California, Chile, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand.

First, the grape. Merlot is a black variety that grows in moderate and warm climates. A single-varietal Merlot is usually dry, with medium acidity and medium tannins: softer and rounder than Cabernet Sauvignon. Its character depends on ripeness. Just-ripe Merlot gives light to medium-bodied wines with fresh red fruit, strawberry and red plum, and a herbaceous touch of green bell pepper. Riper Merlot gives medium to full-bodied wines with cooked black fruit, blackberry and black plum. That riper style comes easily in a warm climate, but it can also be reached in a moderate climate by picking later.

In the winery, Merlot can make outstanding wines on its own, but it is also a famous blending grape. When it is blended with higher-tannin varieties such as Cabernet Sauvignon, it adds red fruit and lowers the overall tannin, so the wine is ready to drink sooner. Both oaked and unoaked styles exist. A light, fruity Merlot has little need for long barrel ageing. A fuller style can gain softness and complexity from oak. And the best Merlot-dominated wines age well, developing notes of dried fruit and tobacco.

Now Bordeaux, Merlot's classic home, in south-west France. The climate is moderate, with plenty of rain from the nearby Atlantic, and Merlot is the region's most widely planted grape. Most wines are blends, mainly of Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon. The proportions depend on the style the producer wants, but also on the soils and on each year's weather: in a year when Cabernet struggles, more Merlot goes into the blend.

Bordeaux is split by the Gironde estuary, where the Garonne and Dordogne rivers meet. West and south of the Gironde and Garonne lies the Left Bank, with the Médoc, Graves and Sauternes, where Cabernet Sauvignon usually leads. North and east of the Gironde and Dordogne lies the Right Bank, whose key districts are Saint-Émilion and Pomerol. Here Merlot is king. The outstanding wines of Saint-Émilion and Pomerol are full-bodied, with pronounced black fruit and oak, and they age well, developing dried fruit and tobacco.

A quick word on Bordeaux labels. The regional appellations, Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur, can use grapes from anywhere in the region, and these wines are usually Merlot-led blends. Bordeaux Supérieur has slightly stricter rules on yields, ageing and minimum alcohol than plain Bordeaux. On the Right Bank, the appellation Saint-Émilion also contains a more prestigious level, Saint-Émilion Grand Cru.

Still in France, Merlot is planted widely in the warm Languedoc-Roussillon. You can find single-varietal Merlot at every quality level, as well as blends with Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache and Syrah, usually labelled Pays d'Oc IGP.

Now California, a source of Merlot in every style and at every quality level. Blends are common, but single-varietal Merlot matters too. Styles range from fruity, medium-bodied wines simply labelled California to concentrated, full-bodied wines from the neighbouring regions of Napa Valley and Sonoma. Californian reds often show pronounced oak flavours, vanilla, coconut and smoke. The best are often aged in new barrels, while high-volume producers may use oak chips or staves.

In Chile, Merlot ripens easily in the warm, dry Central Valley, where high yields of fully ripe fruit are possible every year. This makes the Central Valley an important source of soft, medium-bodied Merlot for high-volume brands meant to be drunk young. But altitude can moderate the heat, so fresher styles are made there too.

In South Africa, Stellenbosch has built a strong reputation for complex, age-worthy reds from the classic Bordeaux grapes, Merlot among them. This mountainous region ranges from moderate to warm, depending on vineyard altitude and the influence of sea breezes. In Australia, Merlot has traditionally been a blending partner for Cabernet Sauvignon in high-quality wines, for example from Margaret River in Western Australia.

In New Zealand, most Merlot comes from Hawke's Bay, on the North Island. The climate is moderate with plentiful rain. Wines range from light and fruity to full-bodied and long-lived, and Merlot appears both on its own and blended with Cabernet Sauvignon. In fact, it is more widely grown there than Cabernet, which needs the warmest sites.

Merlot has sometimes been seen as a grape for high-volume brands, or only as a softener for Cabernet Sauvignon. Today producers around the world show that it can make impressive, complex, long-lived wines on its own. With its medium tannin and medium acidity, it is wonderfully versatile: fresh and unoaked at any price, or powerful and enriched by oak and bottle age.

A memory tip: if Cabernet Sauvignon is a firm handshake, Merlot is a warm hug. Softer tannins, medium acidity, plump plums and berries. And to place it on the map, remember that the Right Bank is the Merlot bank: Saint-Émilion and Pomerol, where the hug is at its richest.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Merlot is a black grape for moderate and warm climates, giving dry wines with medium acidity and medium tannin; just-ripe grapes give red fruit and green pepper, riper grapes give a fuller body and cooked black fruit. Second, it is Bordeaux's most planted grape and leads the Right Bank wines of Saint-Émilion and Pomerol, as well as most Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur, while it softens Cabernet Sauvignon in blends. Third, elsewhere it ranges from fruity, high-volume wines from Pays d'Oc, California and Chile's Central Valley to fuller, oaked wines from Napa Valley and Sonoma, and quality reds and blends from Stellenbosch, Margaret River and Hawke's Bay.
